New Jersey effectively does this. Local districts are funded by local property taxes, but the state also collects additional property taxes into a fund that it then disburses to districts according to need. New Jersey ranks higher than other states in the Northeast on most education measures (standardized tests, graduation rates, rate of students who go on to college, etc) but the cost is absolutely astronomical.

The real problem with education is that there is basically no correlation between the amount a school district spends per pupil, and how well students will do. E.g. New York spends more per pupil than any other state and is barely above average, while states that spend less than half what NY does per pupil do much better. A lot of it has to do with who controls spending and how the money is spent. In states that have a lot of money but also have teachers' unions, most of the money goes to salaries and benefits and not really to programs and facilities.

The reality is that the biggest determining factor for educational success is the family's income. Poor kids in wealthy school districts do poorly in school even though the district is well funded. So trying to fix it by spending a lot of money on every school district is not going to work.
